units.d: Life first: be a sheep shepherded by the Lord before you shepherd others.
The Bible is my standard and the Spirit is my guide: knowing and feeding the sheep by God’s heart.
Then ministry: seeking, visiting, healing and restoring, so the Good Shepherd’s heart flows through us.
Build God’s system: shepherd one another in small groups and raise up the next shepherds.

lessons.title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
lessons.sub: Be a sheep who is shepherded before you become a shepherd of others
lessons.hear:
When many people first take on the role of small group leader or care team member, their first thought is, “How do I lead these people well?” Yet the most famous shepherding passage in the Bible does not begin with “I am a shepherd.” It begins, “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1) David, who wrote this psalm, was himself a shepherd, and later became king of Israel, shepherding a whole nation. But the deepest identity of his whole life was being one sheep in the LORD’s pasture.

The first lesson of shepherding ministry is to return to that identity. Think of a flight attendant. Before takeoff, she always reminds us, “If the oxygen masks drop, put on your own mask first, then help the person next to you.” A shepherd who is running out of oxygen cannot hold anyone up. We often think shepherding means endless giving, and so the more we serve, the drier we get; the drier we get, the more anxious we become, until we are simply forcing ourselves on in our own strength. This is not God’s heart.

In Psalm 23, every verb belongs to the shepherd: “He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.” (Psalm 23:2-3) The sheep does only one thing: follow. The sheep does not have to find its own pasture or drive off the jackals by itself; its responsibility is to stay close to the shepherd. The better you are shepherded, the more room your heart has to shepherd others.

This is what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” Shepherding is ministry, but the source of ministry is life, and the source of life is our relationship with God. In relationships, our relationship with God comes first, then with ourselves, with others and with our work. When you eat your fill in God’s pasture every day and are restored beside still waters, then when you visit people or lead your group, you do not bring your own exhaustion; you bring the Shepherd’s presence.

When David comes to the darkest moment, his tone suddenly changes: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.” (Psalm 23:4) He moves from “he” to “you,” from talking about God to talking to God. A true shepherd is someone who has experienced “you are with me” in his own valley. One day, when you sit with a brother or sister in a hospital bed or in the grief of losing a loved one, the most precious thing you can give is not a set of doctrines but a testimony flowing from your own life: “He walked with me through this too.”
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd thinks, “The sheep need me,” and so puts himself at the center and grows ever more tired. The selfless shepherd knows, “Both the sheep and I need the Good Shepherd,” and so returns to Jesus first to be fed. Our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. A shepherd’s greatest qualification is not ability, but being shepherded by Jesus every day.
think: In Psalm 23, what does the shepherd do for the sheep? Which of these do you need most right now?
Lately in my ministry, am I “shepherded and overflowing,” or “out of oxygen and forcing it”? What are the signs?
Where, and in what way, do I let the Good Shepherd feed me each day?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. I confess that I often rush to shepherd others while forgetting to come to your pasture myself. Forgive me for serving in my own strength. Today I choose to be your sheep first, to lie down quietly before you and let you restore my soul. Comfort me and guide me with your rod and your staff, so that what I receive from you may overflow to every person I shepherd. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Be fed first
Each day, before you serve, spend fifteen minutes in Scripture and prayer and let the Good Shepherd feed you.
Write down your pastures
List three things that restore your soul, such as a passage of Scripture, a worship song or a spiritual companion.
Honestly check your fuel
Rate your current spiritual, emotional and physical condition from 1 to 10. If it is below 5, rest first and ask for help first.
Count his presence in the valley
Recall a low point God walked you through, and write three sentences of testimony you can use to comfort others one day.
Hand the sheep to the Chief Shepherd
Entrust the people you shepherd to Jesus one by one, acknowledging that he is the true Shepherd.
lessons.do: Today, before you serve anyone, spend fifteen minutes reading Psalm 23, changing every “he” to “you” and speaking it to the Lord. Then write a testimony of “God walking with me through the valley” and save it in your Shepherding Journal.
deep: Do shepherds need to be shepherded too?

Of course. Peter called himself “a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1). Even the apostles lived in community, with people praying for them and people reminding them. Every shepherd needs his own pastor, spiritual parents and spiritual companions. A shepherd who refuses to be shepherded is the one most likely to quietly dry up or fall.
I’m so busy. I really don’t have time to be fed first. What can I do?

Busyness is exactly the sign that you need to be fed first. The longer a car has to travel, the more it needs to fill up before it sets out. Start small: five minutes each morning, or listening to a chapter of the Bible on your commute. What matters is not the length of time but the relationship of returning to the Shepherd’s side every day.
lessons.quick: A shepherd’s greatest qualification is not ability, but being shepherded by the Good Shepherd every day.
text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.
He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.
Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil. My cup runs over.
Surely goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the LORD’s house forever.
lessons.keyText: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.

lessons.title: The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
lessons.sub: A selfless shepherd, not a hired hand
lessons.hear:
Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11) Right after this, he describes another kind of person: “He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.” (John 10:12) On ordinary days, the shepherd and the hired hand look exactly the same. Both lead the sheep to pasture; both keep watch beside the fold. The difference only shows on the day the wolf comes.

The hired hand is calculating, “Is this job worth it? Will I get hurt?” The shepherd is thinking, “Will my sheep get hurt?” Jesus gets right to the heart of it: “The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.” (John 10:13) The hired hand’s focus is on himself. This is exactly the self-centered life of the old self: serving in order to get something, and retreating as soon as the cost gets too high.

In the church, “the wolf coming” might be a phone call from a brother or sister in the middle of the night. It might be conflict in your small group, or someone misunderstanding and criticizing you, or simply a person whose ups and downs leave you completely drained. Moments like these reveal whether there is a hired hand or a shepherd inside us.

What is the Good Shepherd’s secret? Jesus said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” (John 10:18) Laying down our lives is not a sacrifice forced out of us; it is a willing choice that flows from love. 321 says that denying ourselves means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. This does not mean becoming a pushover with no boundaries. It means that in every moment of choice, we put the good of the sheep ahead of our own comfort.

But who can do this? On our own, we truly cannot. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) The selfless life is not me trying harder to love; it is letting Jesus, the Good Shepherd, live out his love in me. As we practice 920, living out the selfless “0” toward every “2” we relate to and bearing the “9” fruit of the Spirit, the sheep will hear the Good Shepherd’s voice through us.
lessons.light: The hired hand asks, “What will I lose?” The Good Shepherd asks, “What will the sheep lose?” Self-centered service runs when the wolf comes; selfless service steps forward. Being selfless does not mean there is no “me”; it means letting the Good Shepherd reign as King in me. Whatever I lay down, he himself will make up.
think: In John 10:11-13, what is the difference between the shepherd and the hired hand? When does that difference become visible?
In my ministry, what does “the wolf coming” usually look like? At those times, which one do my reactions resemble more?
How is “denying myself” different from “having no boundaries”? How can I lay down my life with wisdom?
lessons.speak: Jesus, Good Shepherd, thank you for laying down your life for me. I confess that I am often like a hired hand, counting the cost as I serve; when the wolf comes, I want to run and protect myself. Forgive my self-centered heart. I choose to let you live in me and let your love become my love. Holy Spirit, give me wisdom to know when to lay myself down, and how to protect the sheep entrusted to me. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Recognize your wolf
Write down a recent shepherding situation that made you want to run away, and honestly face how you feel.
Ask the right question
When you face that situation, change your question from “What will I lose?” to “What does this person need?”
Lay down one small thing
For one person you shepherd, give up one of your own conveniences, such as spending an extra twenty minutes listening.
Set healthy boundaries
At the same time, write down the boundaries you need, such as referring late-night crises to your pastor and keeping a weekly Sabbath for yourself.
Practice 920
Choose one “2,” and this week deliberately live out one fruit of the Spirit toward him or her. Record what happens.
lessons.do: Today, choose the sheep you most want to “avoid.” Pray for that person for five minutes, then reach out with a caring message or a phone call. Write down your feelings and their response in your Shepherding Journal.
deep: Does shepherding mean always being on call and never saying no?

Jesus laid down his life, but he also often withdrew to the wilderness to pray (Luke 5:16), and there were times he did not respond right away (John 11:6). The Good Shepherd keeps the sheep’s true good in mind; he does not treat every request from the sheep as a command. Wise boundaries, shared responsibility within a team and timely referrals are all part of responsible love.
I feel like I don’t love people nearly enough. Can I still be a shepherd?

Feeling that you don’t love enough is exactly where the selfless life begins. Love is not something we squeeze out of ourselves; “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). Admit your lack every day and ask the Good Shepherd to live in you, and you will be amazed at how he loves people through weak you.
lessons.quick: The difference between a shepherd and a hired hand only shows on the day the wolf comes.
text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep and scatters them.
The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own;
even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep.
I have other sheep which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd.
Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.
No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”
lessons.keyText: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

lessons.title: If You Love Me, Feed My Sheep
lessons.sub: The motive for shepherding is love for Jesus
lessons.hear:
By the Sea of Galilee, beside a charcoal fire, the risen Jesus finished breakfast with Peter. Only days before, Peter had also stood beside a charcoal fire and denied the Lord three times. Now Jesus asked him three times, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” And each time Peter answered, Jesus gave him not a rebuke but a commission: “Feed my lambs.” “Tend my sheep.” “Feed my sheep.”

Jesus did not ask Peter, “Are you capable enough?” or “Will you fall again someday?” He asked only one thing: “Do you love me?” This tells us that the root of shepherding is not a sense of duty, not a title, not our own sense of achievement, but love for Jesus. A mother gets up in the middle of the night to feed her baby, not because she has to clock in, but because she loves her child. Those who love the Lord will naturally love the sheep the Lord loves.

Notice the words Jesus used: “my lambs,” “my sheep.” The sheep did not belong to Peter; they belonged to Jesus. Without realizing it, we often say “my small group” or “my members,” and slowly we begin to treat the sheep as our own track record and our own territory. When the sheep grow, we are proud; when they leave, we are hurt or even angry. This is pride at work: leaving our proper place, grabbing hold of power, and treating what belongs to God as our own. Humility is returning to our proper place: the sheep are the Lord’s, and I am a servant entrusted with them.

The third time, “Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time” (John 21:17). That grief came from a heart whose self-confidence had been torn down. Peter no longer boasted that he would never fall. He only said, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” (John 21:17) It was this broken, humbled Peter, no longer relying on himself, who would later write, “shepherd the flock of God which is among you” (1 Peter 5:2).

Someone who has failed and been restored by the Lord understands best how to shepherd the weak. If you feel you have failed and are unworthy to serve, remember the breakfast beside the charcoal fire. The very person Jesus called again was the one who had denied him. Today he asks you too: “Do you love me?” Your answer is the starting point of your shepherding ministry.
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd says “my small group,” treating the sheep as his own track record. The selfless shepherd says “the Lord’s sheep,” seeing himself as a servant entrusted with them. The motive for shepherding is not to be needed or affirmed, but to love the Lord. Let people be people, let God be God; the sheep are the Lord’s, and so is the glory.
think: Why did Jesus ask Peter, “Do you love me?” rather than asking about his ability?
Have I, without realizing it, come to treat the people I shepherd as “mine”? What effect has that had?
What failures have I experienced, and how has God turned them into grace for shepherding others?
lessons.speak: Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you. I also confess that my love is often mixed with a desire to be affirmed and to have results to show. Forgive me for treating your sheep as mine. Today I hand every person I shepherd back to you again. They are your sheep, and I am only your servant. Heal my failures with the love you showed beside the charcoal fire, and let me feed your sheep because I love you. May all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Answer the question
Be still, and hear Jesus call your name and ask, “Do you love me?” Answer him in your own words.
Change one phrase
This week, deliberately replace “my members” with “the sheep the Lord has entrusted to me,” and notice how your attitude shifts.
Hand back the list
Read aloud the names of the people you shepherd, one by one. After each name, say, “Lord, he is your sheep” or “she is your sheep.”
Discern your motives
List three motives behind your service, and honestly mark which come from love for the Lord and which come from the self-centered life.
Bear fruit from failure
Write down a time the Lord restored you, and get ready to share it someday with someone who is struggling.
lessons.do: Today, write a short letter to Jesus answering his question, “Do you love me?” At the end of the letter, hand the people you shepherd back to him one by one. Save it in your Shepherding Journal.
deep: What is the difference between “feed” and “tend”?

In the original Greek, “feed” (boskō) emphasizes providing food, while “tend” or “shepherd” (poimainō) is broader, including leading, protecting and caring for. Jesus used both with Peter, showing that a shepherd must both feed people with God’s Word and care for and guide them in daily life. 321 shepherding is the same: feeding the life and accompanying in relationship go hand in hand.
I’m so worn out from serving that it feels like I have no love left. What should I do?

Don’t rush to force yourself to love; return to being loved first. Peter’s restoration began with a breakfast Jesus had prepared. Take time to receive the love of the cross afresh, talk with a spiritual companion, and rest for a season if you need to. Once you are filled with love again, the strength to serve will return too.
lessons.quick: The root of shepherding is not duty but love for the Lord; the sheep are his, and I am a servant entrusted with them.
text: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
lessons.keyText: He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

lessons.title: Be an Example to the Flock
lessons.sub: Shepherd according to God’s will, not by lording it over others
lessons.hear:
The same Peter who was restored beside the charcoal fire later wrote, in his old age, to the elders of churches in many places. He did not issue orders with apostolic authority. Instead he said, “I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1). That tone alone is a lesson in shepherding: a shepherd walks alongside the sheep; he does not stand high above them.

Peter then sets out the standard for shepherding: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:2-3) Here are three contrasts, and they expose three temptations: compulsion, dishonest gain and lording it over others.

Compulsion treats shepherding as a chore we cannot get out of; we are present in body but not in heart. Serving voluntarily treats it as the Lord’s grace. Dishonest gain is not only about money; it includes wanting reputation, position or the feeling of being needed. Serving willingly is joy that seeks nothing in return. Lording it over others means using power, pressure or guilt to control people, making the sheep go my way. Being an example means walking ahead, so the sheep can see what Christ looks like.

All three temptations are rooted in pride: leaving our proper place as human beings and grabbing hold of God’s power. Lording it over others is the most obvious; it is trying to take God’s place as master in someone else’s life. Humility lays down power and returns to our proper place: let people be people, let God be God. A shepherd’s authority does not come from a position but from a life. The sheep are willing to follow not because they are being managed, but because they have seen Jesus in you.

Finally, Peter says, “When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away.” (1 Peter 5:4) A shepherd is not the boss, only the Chief Shepherd’s helper. Our reward is not today’s applause but the day the Chief Shepherd appears. This eternal perspective turns us from an earthly point of view to a heavenly one, so that we can be examples to the flock voluntarily, willingly and humbly.
lessons.light: Lording it over others says, “Do it my way.” Being an example says, “I will do it God’s way first.” Pride provokes pride; control only brings rebellion or outward compliance. Humility inspires humility; an example draws out willing followers. The shepherd is not the king; Jesus is King.
think: Of the three contrasts in 1 Peter 5:2-3, which one is closest to the temptation I face right now?
In what ways (pressure, guilt, authority) have I tried to control others? What was the result?
What do the people I shepherd see in me most often?
lessons.speak: Jesus, Chief Shepherd, thank you for entrusting me with shepherding your flock. I confess that sometimes I serve under compulsion, sometimes I want to gain affirmation from my service, and sometimes I want to control others in my own way. Forgive my pride, and help me return to my proper place. Make me serve voluntarily and willingly, not lording it over those entrusted to me, but walking ahead as an example to the flock. I wait for the day you appear; all glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Three mirrors
Use the three pairs, “compulsion / voluntarily, dishonest gain / willingly, lording it over / being an example,” to rate your recent ministry.
Turn commands into invitations
This week, when you talk with your group members, change “You need to…” into “Shall we… together?”
Show them first
Choose something you hope your sheep will do (such as reading the Bible or forgiving), practice it yourself first, and share your experience.
Invite feedback
Humbly ask one group member, “Have I ever made you feel pressured?” Listen quietly without defending yourself.
Fix your eyes on the crown
Write down one kind of human affirmation you long for in ministry. Give it to the Lord, and choose instead to wait for his reward.
lessons.do: Today, find one person you shepherd and humbly ask, “Is there anything in the way I lead that I could do better?” Just listen, don’t defend yourself, and then thank them. Write what you heard in your Shepherding Journal and pray about it.
deep: If I shouldn’t lord it over people, does that mean I can never correct anyone?

No. Paul also urged Timothy to “reprove, rebuke, and exhort” (2 Timothy 4:2). The difference lies in motive and manner. Control seeks to make people do things my way; correction that flows from being an example seeks to make people more like Christ, and it speaks the truth within relationship, with gentleness and respect. Lesson 10 will go deeper into restoration.
I’m not an elder. Does this passage still apply to me?

Yes. Peter wrote to elders, but the principles apply to everyone entrusted with caring for others: small group leaders, care team members, parents and workplace managers. Wherever someone follows you, you are a shepherd, and you can be an example to the flock.
lessons.quick: A shepherd’s authority comes not from position but from life; not by lording it over others, but by being an example.
text: Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and who will also share in the glory that will be revealed:
shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly;
not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.
When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away.
lessons.keyText: shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.

lessons.title: He Calls His Own Sheep by Name
lessons.sub: Know your sheep and build 235 spiritual relationships
lessons.hear:
In ancient Israel, the sheep of several families were often kept in the same fold overnight. In the morning, the shepherd came to the gate and called out, and his own sheep would come out from the mixed flock. Jesus said, “The sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” (John 10:3) The shepherd knows every sheep, even by name; and the sheep know the shepherd’s voice. “They will by no means follow a stranger” (John 10:5).

Shepherding is a relationship, not a management system. Proverbs says, “Know well the state of your flocks” (Proverbs 27:23). A good shepherd knows not only the names of the group members but also their families, work, struggles, dreams and spiritual condition. He knows who has not been sleeping well lately, whose child is going through a rebellious stage, and who has just changed jobs. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Don’t let the progress of ministry make you overlook the person right in front of you.

Knowing the sheep takes time, and it takes care. Many small group leaders meet with their groups for two hours every week, yet have never shared a meal alone with a single member. Sheep do not learn the shepherd’s voice during meetings. They learn it gradually, through one act of care after another, one phone call after another, one season of companionship after another, until they recognize, “This is someone who loves me.”

321’s 235 relationships give us a clear path. First, become a “2,” spiritual companions, with someone who is healthy and selfless, supporting each other. Next, build “3” relationships of spiritual parents and children, with someone leading ahead of you and someone following behind. Finally, become “5,” spiritual comrades, forming a team in the fivefold ministry to build God’s system together. Shepherding is not one person leading a crowd; it is a web of relationships, layer upon layer, joined by life.

Jesus said the shepherd “goes before them; and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice” (John 10:4). Sheep do not follow commands; they follow a familiar voice. Do the people you shepherd recognize your voice today? More importantly, in your voice, can they hear the voice of Jesus, the Good Shepherd?
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd values numbers and activities, treating people as figures on a list. The selfless shepherd values every name, treating people as lives entrusted by the Lord. When our focus is on Jesus, we will also see each person the way Jesus sees them. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.
think: In John 10:3-5, what signs show that the shepherd and the sheep “know” each other?
Can I name the biggest recent need of each person I shepherd? Who is the one I know least?
In terms of 235 relationships, do I currently have spiritual companions and spiritual parents? Whose spiritual parent am I?
lessons.speak: Jesus, Good Shepherd, thank you for calling me by name; you know me more deeply than I know myself. Give me a shepherd’s heart to know well the state of my flock, not treating people as numbers but as lives precious to you. Help me build relationships with spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and spiritual comrades, so that in my voice your sheep may hear your voice. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Make a file for each sheep
In My Flock, add an entry for each person you shepherd and write down how they are doing right now.
Fill in a knowing map
For each person, write down: family, work, current struggles, spiritual condition and one prayer request.
Find your blind spot
Mark the person you know least, and this week arrange a one-on-one coffee or call.
Draw your 235
Draw your relationship map: who are your 2 spiritual companions, your 3 spiritual parents and children, and your 5 spiritual comrades.
Pray by name
Pray for your sheep by name every day, asking the Holy Spirit to show you each person’s needs.
lessons.do: Today, open My Flock and add the people you shepherd one by one, with one line about how each is doing. Then pick the person you know least and set up a time to meet or talk this week.
deep: How many people can one small group leader shepherd?

Jesus had the seventy, the twelve disciples and three core disciples. Moses’ father-in-law Jethro advised appointing “rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens” (Exodus 18:21). Generally speaking, one person can deeply shepherd about five to twelve people. Beyond that, more shepherds need to be raised up, forming layer upon layer of 235 relationships, which is the theme of Lesson 12.
If I get too close to my group members, will I lose my authority as a shepherd?

Spiritual authority comes from life and love, not from distance. Jesus ate and lived with his disciples, yet he did not lose his authority. What needs attention is boundaries: no favoritism, no exclusive cliques, and appropriate distance between men and women. Closeness is meant to bring people to Jesus, not to bring them to ourselves.
lessons.quick: Shepherding is a relationship, not a management system; the Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name.
text: “Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber.
But one who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
Whenever he brings out his own sheep, he goes before them; and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.
They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.”
lessons.keyText: The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.

lessons.title: Feed the Sheep with God’s Word
lessons.sub: The Bible is my standard and the sheep’s food
lessons.hear:
A shepherd’s most basic task is to make sure the sheep are well fed. What sheep eat shapes what they become. Paul reminded his spiritual son Timothy, “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.” (2 Timothy 3:16-17) The most important tool in a shepherd’s hand is not his own experience or psychological techniques, but God’s Word.

These four ways Scripture is “profitable” are exactly the four dimensions of shepherding. Teaching tells people what is true. Reproof points out where they have strayed. Correction helps them back onto the right path. Instruction in righteousness walks with them as they practice the way of righteousness and form new habits. Think of a mountain guide: first he tells you the route; when he sees you going the wrong way, he warns you; he brings you back to the trail; and then he walks with you all the way to the summit.

Much shepherding loses its way because it gradually becomes all comfort and no truth, or all truth and no love. Shepherding that offers only comfort is like handing out candy: the sheep are happy for a moment, but they never grow up. Shepherding that offers only truth is like forcing down a huge piece of raw meat: the sheep cannot swallow it. A good shepherd cuts God’s Word into portions the sheep can eat, according to their condition: milk for new believers, solid food for the mature.

Paul also said, “But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them.” (2 Timothy 3:14) Timothy learned his faith from the lives of his grandmother, his mother and Paul. God’s Word is passed on not only through explanation but even more through life. A shepherd must first be changed by God’s Word before he can use God’s Word to change others. Change the way people think, and you change their lives; change their lives, and you change how they live.

So every care visit and every one-on-one can be an occasion to bring a verse along. Not to lecture, but to hand someone a mouthful of God’s bread at the moment they need it most. That is what the Care Verses in this course are for. As you grow used to shepherding with God’s Word, you will discover that what truly changes people has never been our words, but God’s Word and the work of the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd shepherds with his own opinions, and in the end the sheep follow only the shepherd. The selfless shepherd shepherds with God’s Word, and in the end the sheep follow Jesus. The Bible is my standard and the Holy Spirit is my guide. The shepherd is not the food, only the pair of hands that passes the food to the sheep.
think: What does each of the four ways Scripture is “profitable” in 2 Timothy 3:16 look like in shepherding? Which do I use most, and which least?
Does my shepherding lean more toward “only comfort” or “only truth”?
Which verse has changed me recently? How could I share it with one of my sheep?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for giving your God-breathed Word, so that those who belong to you may be complete. I confess that I often shepherd people with my own experience and opinions, and seldom with your Word. Feed me and change me with your Word first, and then enable me to cut your Word into portions each person can take in, according to their needs. Holy Spirit, guide me to say the right thing at the right time, so that people may receive life through your Word. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Eat before you feed
Each week as you read the Bible, pick one verse to put into practice yourself first; that becomes the “food” you share with your sheep that week.
Build a pocket of verses
Choose five verses from Care Verses and memorize them, so they are ready to use in care at any time.
Match the food to the sheep
For each of your sheep, discern whether they need teaching, reproof, correction or companionship in instruction in righteousness right now.
Ask instead of lecture
When you share a verse, use questions instead of conclusions: “As you read this verse, what touched you?”
Practice it together
Agree with one of your sheep to practice one verse together for seven days, and share with each other on the eighth day.
lessons.do: Today, choose a verse from Care Verses that fits one of your sheep. Use Xiaozhi to write a blessing, turn it into a scripture image and send it to them with the words, “I thought of you today and prayed for you.”
deep: I’m not a seminary student. What if I misinterpret Scripture?

When we share Scripture in shepherding, the point is not deep exegesis, but being faithful to the original meaning of the text and humbly sharing what you have received. Choose verses whose meaning is clear. When you are not sure, say, “This is how I understand it,” and talk it over with your pastor or a spiritual companion. Continuing to read whole books of the Bible and joining Bible studies will also give you growing confidence.
When someone is in pain, should I quote Scripture?

It depends on the timing. When people are in deep pain, sometimes what they need most is companionship, not a verse: “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Listen, stay with them and pray first. When they are ready, gently offer them a promise. Don’t use Scripture to stop someone’s tears.
lessons.quick: What truly changes people is not our words, but God’s Word and the work of the Holy Spirit.
text: But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them.
From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
lessons.keyText: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

lessons.title: Seeking the Lost Sheep
lessons.hear:
The Pharisees saw that “all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him,” and they murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them” (Luke 15:1-2). So Jesus told them a parable: “Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?” (Luke 15:4)

On a shepherd’s ledger, ninety-nine is already an impressive number, and a one percent loss might seem acceptable. But the Good Shepherd doesn’t count that way. To him, that one sheep is not “one percent”; it is a life with a name, deeply loved and irreplaceable. People matter more than tasks, and in God’s eyes, people matter far more than numbers.

The lost sheep in a church usually disappear quietly: first they come late, then they miss now and then, then messages are “seen” but never answered, and finally they are gone altogether. Very often they haven’t stopped loving the Lord. They have been hurt, they are going through hardship, they feel overlooked, or they are ashamed of sin and afraid to come back. If no one goes looking for them, they wander farther and farther into the wilderness.

Notice the detail Jesus gives: when the shepherd finds the sheep, he doesn’t scold it or lecture it. “When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:5). A lost sheep is often exhausted and frightened, too weak to walk; the shepherd lifts it onto his shoulders and carries it home with his own strength. When we go looking for someone who has drifted away, our first words should not be “Why haven’t you been coming?” but “I’ve really missed you. How are you doing?”

This takes a selfless heart. Going after a lost sheep may mean being rejected, met with coldness, or misunderstood. The self-centered person says, “He’s the one who stopped coming.” But the selfless person remembers that Jesus once came looking for me in exactly this way. “There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance” (Luke 15:7). Every time you go looking for one sheep, you are taking part on earth in the joy of heaven.
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd sees the ninety-nine and thinks that is good enough; the selfless shepherd sees the one and cannot rest. From a human point of view, it is an acceptable loss; from God’s point of view, it is a name heaven is waiting to rejoice over. When our focus is on Jesus, we will see the people Jesus is seeking.
think: In Luke 15:4-6, what does the Good Shepherd do after he finds the sheep? Which one moves you most?
Among the people I shepherd, who is slowly “disappearing”? When did I last contact them?
What is my biggest obstacle to going after someone who has drifted away?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, thank you that you once left the ninety-nine to come looking for me, and carried me home on your shoulders. Put your seeking heart within me, so that I never treat any sheep as expendable. Bring to my mind those who have quietly slipped away, and give me courage and gentleness to go after them. If I am rejected, keep my heart from bitterness; when they are found, let the joy of heaven fill us. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Take roll
Open My Flock and mark everyone you haven’t been in touch with for more than two weeks.
Pray first, then reach out
Pray for that person, asking the Holy Spirit to prepare their heart and to prepare the words you will say.
Send “I miss you”
Begin your message with “I’ve missed you.” Don’t ask why they’ve been absent; simply show that you care.
Carry them on your shoulders
If they are willing to meet, go to a place convenient for them, listen to their story, and don’t rush to urge them to come back.
Rejoice together
If they return, welcome them warmly in your small group, without making them feel awkward.
lessons.do: Today, find the person in My Flock you haven’t contacted for the longest time. Pray for them first, then send a message: “It’s been so long. I really miss you. How have you been?” Whether or not they reply, make a note in your care records and keep praying for them.
deep: They’ve told me clearly they don’t want to come to church anymore. Should I still go after them?

Respect their choice: don’t pester them or pressure them. But you can keep the friendship and keep caring, sending a blessing at holidays, on their birthday, or when they are in need. Seeking doesn’t necessarily mean pulling them back into meetings; it means letting them know someone still loves them and prays for them. Many people return to the Lord years later precisely because they remember someone who never gave up on them.
If we leave the ninety-nine to look for the one, what happens to the ninety-nine?

The point of the parable is how much the Good Shepherd treasures each person, not that we should neglect everyone else. In real shepherding, this is exactly why we need a team: some care for the sheep in the gathering, while others go out to seek. It is also why we raise up more shepherds and build a 235 team of spiritual comrades.
lessons.quick: In God’s eyes, that one sheep is not one percent; it is a name heaven is waiting to rejoice over.
text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him.
The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”
He told them this parable:
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
lessons.keyText: “Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?

lessons.title: Weeping with Those Who Weep
lessons.sub: Care visits: presence instead of preaching
lessons.hear:
When Paul describes how Christians love one another, his first words are: “Let love be without hypocrisy” (Romans 12:9). What follows is a string of very down-to-earth reminders, and one of them belongs on the heart of every caregiver: “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).

The biggest challenge in a care visit is often not that we don’t know what to say, but that we are in too much of a hurry to say something. When we see someone in pain, we rush to explain why, offer solutions, and quote verses, as if we had to dry their tears as quickly as possible. Job’s three friends started out well: “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (Job 2:13). But as soon as they opened their mouths, they began to analyze and condemn, and in the end even God said they had not spoken what was right.

To weep with someone means stepping into their situation rather than standing on the shore teaching them how to swim. Picture someone who has fallen into a deep well. Self-centered care shouts down from the top: “Here’s how you should climb out!” Selfless care lowers a ladder, climbs down, sits beside them, and says, “I’m here with you.” Then together they look up to the God who is able to lift us out.

Paul also says: “Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble” (Romans 12:16). Care visits require humility: not carrying an attitude of “I’m more spiritual than you,” not rushing to give answers, but admitting, “I don’t fully understand either, but I’m willing to be with you.” Very often a quiet hug, a bowl of hot soup, or a simple “I’ll keep praying for you” lets a person feel God’s love more than a whole sermon could.

The ministry practice in this lesson will teach you the Six Steps of Care Visits: prepare yourself; greet with love and listen; empathize and comfort; feed them with God’s word; pray and bless; record and follow up. These steps are not a formula; they help you let Jesus be Lord in every visit. Remember, you are not the hero who goes to fix the problem; you are the servant who goes to keep someone company. The true Comforter is the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: Self-centered care hurries to speak, wanting to prove it is helpful; selfless care is willing to be quiet, so the other person feels understood. Humility inspires humility: when we stoop down to the lowly, they finally dare to open their true hearts. We are not the answer; Jesus is. We are simply the ones walking with them toward Jesus.
think: In Romans 12:9-16, which sentence most challenges my habits when I care for people?
When others are in pain, what mistake am I most likely to make (lecturing, explaining, changing the subject)?
When I was low, what did someone do that truly comforted me?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, our Comforter, thank you that when I was hurting most, you did not rebuke me but stayed with me. Forgive me for so often rushing to speak and rushing to fix, without truly listening. Give me a humble heart that weeps with others, so that I can stoop down to the lowly, sit beside them, and let them feel your love through my presence. Be the comfort of everyone who suffers. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Prepare yourself
Pray before the visit, learn about the person’s situation, and have a verse ready, but don’t rush to use it.
Greet with love
Open with an open-ended question: “How have things been for you lately?” Then listen quietly.
Respond with empathy
Reflect their feelings with “It sounds like you’re really…” and don’t rush to give advice.
Offer a bite of bread
When they are ready, gently share a promise from Scripture, or read a psalm together.
Pray and follow up
With their permission, pray for them; afterward, record their needs and check in again within three days.
lessons.do: Today, use the Six Steps of Care Visits to prepare a visit or a care phone call. Choose someone going through a hard time, pray first, then contact them, and this time do just one thing: listen more and talk less. Afterward, write it down in your care records.
deep: They keep crying and I don’t know what to say. What should I do?

When you don’t know what to say, don’t force yourself to speak. You can say, “I’m here with you,” or “Take your time,” or simply stay quietly beside them and hand them a tissue. Silence is not failure; it is respect. At the end, you can ask, “May I pray for you?” and entrust them to God with a short prayer.
When should a caregiver refer someone for professional help?

When the person has thoughts of harming themselves or others, is experiencing violence, shows signs of serious depression or mental illness, has long-term insomnia that keeps them from functioning, or faces legal or medical decisions, first make sure they are safe, then encourage and help them seek professional help, and let your pastor know. Referral is not a lack of love; it is a more responsible love.
lessons.quick: You are not the hero who goes to fix the problem, but the servant who goes to keep company; the true Comforter is the Holy Spirit.
text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.
lessons.keyText: Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

lessons.title: Binding Up the Injured, Healing the Sick
lessons.sub: Supporting weak sheep according to God’s heart
lessons.hear:
Ezekiel 34 contains the Bible’s sternest rebuke of shepherds. God charges the shepherds of Israel: “You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor” (Ezekiel 34:4). They fed only themselves, treating the sheep as resources to supply their own needs.

Then God says something deeply moving: “Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). God did not give up on his sheep; he would be their shepherd himself. And finally he promises: “I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick” (Ezekiel 34:16). This is a complete reversal of verse 4: everything the negligent shepherds failed to do, God himself does, one by one.

This verse is like a job description written by God’s own hand for shepherds. The church has all kinds of weak sheep. Some are frail in faith and need to be slowly built up. Some are sick in body or soul and need healing and companionship. Some are wounded in relationships and need their wounds bound up. Some have been driven away by conflict or a fall and need to be brought back. Some are already lost and need to be sought. Each need calls for a different kind of care.

Binding up wounds takes patience. Like bandaging an injury, too much force makes it hurt more, and too little care lets it get infected. Healing also takes time; you can’t bandage someone today and send them into battle tomorrow. Many wounded people don’t need pressure to “hurry up and get better.” They need a season of safe time and space where God can heal them gently.

When God says “I myself,” it reminds us that the true Healer is God, not us. We are not here to play savior, but to let the Good Shepherd bind up and heal through our hands. The selfless shepherd knows his own limits, so he relies all the more on the Holy Spirit, and is all the more glad to work with a team and to refer people to professionals. Let people be people, let God be God; then all the glory for healing goes to God.
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd feeds only himself, using the sheep as tools to build his own ministry; the selfless shepherd lives for the sheep, offering himself as God’s healing hands. Since God says “I myself,” we don’t have to pretend to be the savior; we only need to obey and let him work through us.
think: Comparing Ezekiel 34:4 with 34:16, what are the five things God says he will do himself?
Among the people I shepherd, who is weak, sick, injured, driven away, or lost?
Have I ever, without realizing it, been “feeding only myself”? What did that look like?
lessons.speak: God, our own Shepherd, thank you that you never give up on your sheep, and you never give up on me. I confess that I have sometimes cared only about my own ministry and overlooked weak and wounded sheep. Please forgive me. Make me your hands: to strengthen the weak, to stay beside the sick, to bind up the injured, to bring back those driven away, and to seek the lost. I know that you are the one who heals, not me; may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Discern each sheep’s condition
Using the five conditions in Ezekiel 34:16, sort each person in My Flock into a category.
The weak: feed them
Arrange one-on-one Bible reading with those whose faith is frail, one passage a week.
The sick: stay with them
Pray for the sick, visit them, offer practical help (meals, rides), and respect their medical care.
The injured: bind them up
Give the wounded a safe space to express their feelings, without pushing them to forgive or let go right away.
The driven away and the lost: bring them back
Reach out to those who left because of conflict or a fall, show them acceptance, and invite your pastor to come along when needed.
lessons.do: Today, sort the people you shepherd using the five conditions in Ezekiel 34:16, choosing the matching category in My Flock. Pick one person from each category and write down one specific act of care you will do next.
deep: I prayed for someone who was sick and they weren’t healed. How should I respond?

Healing is in God’s sovereign hands. We pray in the Lord’s name and believe God is able to heal, but don’t promise anyone “you will definitely get better,” and never say “your faith wasn’t strong enough.” Sometimes God heals immediately, sometimes slowly through medical care, and sometimes completely in eternity. Whatever happens, being with them is itself love, and a sign of God’s presence.
Someone who’s been hurt keeps staying in their pain. How long should I walk with them?

Healing takes time, and everyone heals at a different pace. Walk with them gently, and help them bring their pain to God step by step. If the pain is seriously affecting daily life, or involves trauma or depression, encourage them to seek professional counseling. A shepherd’s role is to accompany and connect people with resources, not to carry everything alone.
lessons.quick: Where negligent shepherds failed, God says “I myself”; we are simply his healing hands.
text: For the Lord GOD says: “Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.

As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so I will seek out my sheep. I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.

I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the watercourses, and in all the inhabited places of the country.
I will feed them with good pasture; and their fold will be on the mountains of the height of Israel. There they will lie down in a good fold. They will feed on fat pasture on the mountains of Israel.
I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down,” says the Lord GOD.

I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick; but I will destroy the fat and the strong. I will feed them in justice.
lessons.keyText: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick; but I will destroy the fat and the strong. I will feed them in justice.

lessons.title: Restoring with a Gentle Spirit
lessons.sub: Speaking the truth in love, bearing one another’s burdens
lessons.hear:
One of the hardest moments in shepherding is facing someone who has fallen. Paul says: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). In this one sentence we find the goal, the attitude, and the warning of restoration.

The goal is to “restore.” The original word was also used for fishermen mending torn nets, or for a doctor setting a dislocated bone back into place. Restoration is not punishment, not exposure, not driving someone out; it is repairing a person so they can return to where they belong. If, when we face someone who has fallen, we are thinking, “Now his true colors have finally come out,” that is not restoration; it is judgment.

The attitude is “a spirit of gentleness.” Gentleness is not weakness; it is strength under control. Like a doctor setting a bone, you must push it firmly back into place, but your hands must be precise and gentle. Speak the truth in love: don’t cover up sin, and don’t humiliate the person; talk privately first, rather than accusing them in public; listen first, then speak; point out the problem, and also point to the grace of the cross.

The warning is “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Those who restore others are the most prone to pride, thinking, “I would never be like him.” Paul goes on: “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Galatians 6:3). That is exactly the danger of pride. A humble restorer knows that if it weren’t for God’s grace, he could fall just the same. Pride against pride, both lose; humility inspires humility, and both win.

Paul also says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Restoration doesn’t end with a single conversation; it is followed by a long season of walking together. Someone who has fallen needs others to share the load, to pray with them, and to help them stand up again. This is the body of Christ: no one fights alone.
lessons.light: When the self-centered person sees someone fall, what rises in the heart is “I’m better than him”; when the selfless person sees someone fall, the thought is “that could be me.” Humility overcomes pride: only those who have received grace themselves can gently carry grace to the fallen. The goal of restoration is not to prove who is right, but to bring a person back to Jesus.
think: In Galatians 6:1, what are the goal, the attitude, and the warning of restoration?
When facing someone who has done wrong, am I more likely to judge harshly, or to avoid talking about it altogether?
Have I ever been gently restored by someone? What did that person do?
lessons.speak: Gracious Lord, thank you that when I fell, you did not cast me away but gently restored me. Search my heart; remove the pride that judges others, and remove the weakness that fears conflict and won’t speak the truth. Give me a gentle spirit and spiritual wisdom to speak the truth in love, and a willingness to bear burdens with the fallen for the long haul. Keep me as well, so that I am not tempted. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Examine yourself first
Before the conversation, examine yourself before God: Is there any judgment, anger, or desire to prove myself right in my heart?
Talk gently in private
Choose a private, safe setting, open with “I really care about you,” and listen to their side first.
State facts, not labels
Describe specific behaviors and their impact; don’t say, “You’re just that kind of person.”
Point to the cross
Acknowledge the seriousness of sin, and also declare: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Bear the burden together
Agree on how you will keep walking together and how they will be accountable, keep praying for them, and involve your pastor when needed.
lessons.do: Today, think about whether there is someone who needs to be restored and whom you have been avoiding. First spend ten minutes praying for them and for yourself, then write down your opening words and one verse, and ask Xiaozhi to help you check whether your tone is gentle.
deep: What if the person won’t admit it or repent?

In Matthew 18:15-17, Jesus gives the steps: first speak with them privately; if they don’t listen, take one or two others along; if they still won’t listen, tell it to the church. This is a gradual, careful process whose goal is restoration. Those who serve in shepherding should not handle serious sin alone; face it together with your pastor and church leaders, and keep praying for the person.
If it involves harming others (such as domestic violence or sexual assault), is gentle restoration still all that’s needed?

No. When harm to others or illegal conduct is involved, the first priority is protecting the victim’s safety, reporting to the proper authorities when necessary, and seeking professional help. The repentance of the one who caused harm still matters, but never ask the victim to endure or keep silent in the name of “forgiveness” or “restoration.” Your pastor must be informed immediately in situations like these.
lessons.quick: Restoration is not proving who is right, but bringing a person back to Jesus with a gentle spirit.
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.
lessons.keyText: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

lessons.title: A Community Breaking Bread at Home
lessons.sub: Small group shepherding: loving and shepherding one another
lessons.hear:
After the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost, the early church grew by three thousand people in a single day. With so many people, how could the apostles shepherd them? Luke records their life together: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer” (Acts 2:42). And “day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home” (Acts 2:46). In the temple they gathered as a large assembly; at home they gathered in small groups. The large gathering gives people vision; the small gathering gives people shepherding.

These four things are the four pillars of a healthy small group. The apostles’ teaching is feeding on God’s word. Fellowship is sharing life and supporting one another. The breaking of bread is remembering the Lord, and it also includes the real life of eating together. Prayer is coming before God together. Just as a table needs four legs to stand firmly, a small group that only studies the Bible becomes a book club, and one that only chats becomes a social club. Only when all four are present is it truly God’s family.

Most beautiful of all, shepherding in the early church did not depend on the apostles alone; they shepherded one another. “All who believed were together” (Acts 2:44), and when anyone was in need, everyone helped. A small group leader is not the only shepherd, but a shepherd who helps every member learn to care for one another, pray for one another, and carry one another’s burdens. When a small group becomes a community that shepherds one another, the leader won’t burn out.

And the result? “They took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:46-47). Notice that it was “the Lord” who added people to them. We don’t grow a small group through technique; we live out a community full of love, truth, and the presence of the Holy Spirit. When people see Jesus among us, the Lord himself will bring them in.

This lesson’s tool, Small Group Guides, will help you lead gatherings that include welcome, worship, God’s word, praying for one another, and sending out. But more important than any guide is that every member is selfless: not fighting over who is right, not competing to speak, but deferring to one another. Only selflessness brings unity, only unity brings victory, and only then can we build God’s system.
lessons.light: A self-centered small group revolves around the leader, or around its own needs; a selfless small group revolves around Jesus. Only selflessness brings unity, and a united community naturally draws people in. It is not we who make the group grow; the Lord adds to us day by day those who are being saved, and the glory belongs to him.
think: Of the four pillars in Acts 2:42, which is strongest in my small group? Which is weakest?
Is my small group a place where “the leader shepherds everyone,” or where “everyone shepherds one another”?
How can a newcomer feel the warmth of home the moment they walk into our small group?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for placing us in your household. Make our small group like the early church, continuing steadfastly in your teaching, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayer. Remove the self-centeredness and strife among us, so that we are of one accord and love one another with gladness and singleness of heart. Make every member a shepherd to one another, and add to us day by day those who are being saved. All glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Check the four pillars
Score your small group on the four pillars: teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer.
Hold a love feast
Plan a gathering around a shared meal, so that life and faith are woven together.
Share the shepherding
Divide members into prayer partners of two or three who check in on and pray for one another each week.
Let people take part
At each gathering, invite different people to lead worship, Scripture reading, and prayer, so more people learn to serve.
Be ready for newcomers
Assign a warm co-worker to welcome first-time guests and to follow up with them within a week.
lessons.do: Today, use Small Group Guides to prepare for your next small group gathering. Pair up the members as prayer partners, send everyone the pairings, and invite them to check in with each other once this week.
deep: In my small group, one person talks constantly and another never speaks. What should I do?

At the start, you can explain that “everyone shares one sentence first,” and use taking turns so everyone has a chance. For those who talk a lot, thank them privately for their engagement and ask them to help encourage others to speak up. For quiet members, invite them with simple, non-threatening questions without forcing them. The best example is for the leader to talk less first.
When conflict arises between small group members, how should the leader handle it?

First listen to each side privately, and don’t deal with it publicly in the group chat. Help them see each other’s needs rather than fight to win. Encourage those involved to talk directly, following the principle of Matthew 18:15, and go with them if needed. If the conflict is serious or involves harm, ask your pastor for help. Remember, the goal is reconciliation, not deciding who is right.
lessons.quick: The large gathering gives vision; the small gathering gives shepherding; the Lord adds to us day by day those who are being saved.
text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.
lessons.keyText: Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.title: Entrusting Faithful People Who Can Teach Others
lessons.sub: Raising up shepherds, building God’s system
lessons.hear:
In the final season of his life, Paul wrote to his spiritual son Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). In this one verse there are four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others. The highest goal of shepherding is not how many sheep we shepherd ourselves, but how many shepherds we raise up.

Imagine a relay race. No matter how fast a runner is, if the baton is dropped, the whole team loses. In many churches, shepherding stops at the first generation: one capable small group leader does everything himself, and the members grow more and more dependent on him. Then one day he burns out or moves away, and the whole group falls apart. That is not successful shepherding; it is shepherding that never multiplies.

Paul chose people who were “faithful.” Faithfulness matters more than ability: being faithful in small things, teachable, of good character, loving the Lord and loving people. Ability can be developed, but character takes time to see. This is the 235 of 321: first we become 2 spiritual companions, getting to know each other as we walk together; then we build 3 relationships of spiritual parents and children, intentionally accompanying and equipping; and finally together we become 5 spiritual comrades, forming a fivefold ministry team to build God’s system together.

Paul uses three pictures to describe such people. The soldier: “No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life” (2 Timothy 2:4). The athlete: “He isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules” (2 Timothy 2:5). The farmer: “The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops” (2 Timothy 2:6). The soldier stands for single-minded focus, the athlete for discipline, and the farmer for patience. Raising up shepherds requires all three: wholehearted commitment, training by the rules, and patience as we wait for life to mature.

And the source of strength for all of this is the first verse: “You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:1). Not strong in ourselves, but strong in grace. When you begin to pass the baton, remember: you are not trying to make copies of yourself, but to help the next generation become more like Jesus. Only the selfless can build God’s system; only the selfless can build God’s Kingdom. As generation after generation of shepherds is raised up, the Lord’s Prayer will be fulfilled: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).
lessons.light: The self-centered shepherd wants to be needed and keeps the sheep close to himself; the selfless shepherd wants to be replaced and hands the baton to the next generation. Successful shepherding is not measured by how many people follow me, but by how many can go and shepherd others. The Kingdom, the power, and the glory all belong to God.
think: What four generations appear in 2 Timothy 2:2? Which generation am I in right now?
Are there “faithful people who can teach others” around me? How can I recognize and develop them?
If I had to leave tomorrow, would the people I shepherd continue to be cared for?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for entrusting your sheep to me, and thank you for strengthening me in your grace. I confess that I sometimes want to be needed and am reluctant to hand over the ministry. Remove my self-centered heart; give me eyes to see faithful people, and patience to walk with them and equip them. Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. May shepherds be raised up generation after generation, and may all glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray. Amen.
prac: Find your Timothy
After praying, write down the names of one or two people you see as faithful and eager to learn.
Invite them alongside
Invite them to serve with you, starting with visiting together or leading part of a gathering together.
I do, you watch
Help them grow through five steps: “I do, you watch; I do, you help; you do, I help; you do, I watch; you do, someone else watches.”
Give them the tools
Share this app’s lessons and tools with them, and go through one lesson together each week.
Let go and bless
Set a time for them to begin leading a small group or caring for a sheep, while you stand alongside to support and pray.
lessons.do: Today, pray for a faithful person near you, then invite them to join you next time for a visit or to lead one part of a small group gathering. Share this app with them, and agree to start learning together from Lesson 1.
deep: I’m not mature enough myself. Can I really disciple others?

Yes. Timothy was young too, yet Paul still told him to entrust what he had learned to others. You don’t have to be perfect; you only need to be one step ahead and faithfully pass on what you have received from the Lord. In the process of developing others, you yourself will grow even more.
What if the people I train end up more gifted than I am? Will I feel let down?

If you feel let down, that is exactly the opportunity to practice selflessness. John the Baptist said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Seeing the next generation surpass you is the greatest joy of spiritual parents. The glory doesn’t go to us, or to them, but entirely to Jesus.
lessons.quick: The highest goal of shepherding is not how many sheep we shepherd, but how many shepherds we raise up.
text: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.
Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.
lessons.keyText: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

verses.v: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
verses.p: Listen to their worries first, then help them hand each one to God, sentence by sentence.

verses.v: Praise the LORD, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name! Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits, who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies, who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
verses.p: Count God’s benefits together, pray for healing of body and soul, and encourage them to keep seeing their doctor.

verses.v: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
verses.p: Say less, stay longer. Let them know the LORD is near the brokenhearted, and that you will be there too.

verses.v: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
verses.p: Invite them to rest in Jesus first, then ask: which burden could you lay down this week?

verses.v: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
verses.p: Read the promise to them with their name in it: God is with you and will uphold you.

verses.v: Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”
verses.p: Remind them God will never forsake them, and show it by setting a time to meet again.

verses.v: Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
verses.p: Ask about practical needs first, then seek God’s Kingdom together and pray for the next step.

verses.v: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verses.p: Restore gently: God is faithful and will forgive, and you are not alone.

verses.v: He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.
verses.p: Don’t rush them to forgive. First let them know God heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.

verses.v: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me.
verses.p: Lead with “I miss you,” not blame: Jesus is still knocking at the door, and you miss them too.

verses.v: If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
